query: For multicomponent high-entropy alloys in solid and liquid states at and near their high melting temperatures, what single testable methodological intervention could overcome the inability of EAM references to represent the many atomic configurations of the ab initio liquid? Explain why it should improve reference–target phase-space overlap, predict the reduction in thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD’s EAM references, define the applicable composition and temperature ranges, identify supporting evidence from elemental or binary calculations, and specify a decisive free-energy benchmark that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: An actively learned machine‐learning interatomic potential (e.g., a deep neural network or moment tensor potential) trained on ab initio liquid configurations of multicomponent high-entropy alloys can serve as a far superior reference than the traditional EAM, by capturing the full diversity of local atomic environments present in the liquid and near-melting solid states.
generation.material_initial_state: Multicomponent (e.g., equimolar five-component) high-entropy alloys in both solid and liquid states near their melting temperatures.
generation.intervention: Replace the conventional EAM potential used in thermodynamic integration (as in TOR-TILD) with an actively learned machine-learning interatomic potential that is trained specifically on ab initio configurations sampled at high temperature (around melting) so as to better reflect the many atomic motifs present in the liquid.
generation.conditions: Applicable for refractory high-entropy alloys working near their high melting temperatures (approximately 0.9–1.1×Tₘ), where the liquid phase exhibits extensive configurational diversity. The method is tailored for multicomponent, near-equimolar compositions that display strong chemical disorder.
generation.structural_mediator: The machine learning potential provides a smoother and more accurate representation of the varying local atomic environments (i.e. the configurational entropy) in both the liquid and near-melting solid phases, improving the overlap between the reference and target phase spaces.
generation.mechanism: Unlike EAM models—which have limited ability to represent many-body and chemical complexities—the ML potential is trained by active sampling of ab initio data, thereby capturing a broader range of atomic configurations. This enhanced representation reduces the mismatch along the thermodynamic integration path and thus improves the free-energy estimation.
generation.predicted_outcome: A significant reduction in the thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD’s EAM references, with a predicted improvement (e.g., a reduction in integration errors by roughly 30–50% on a relative scale) leading to more accurate computed free energy differences.
generation.baseline: TOR-TILD’s existing methodology using conventional EAM potentials, which are known to inadequately sample the wide configurational space of the ab initio liquid in high-entropy systems.
generation.boundary: The approach is expected to work well in compositions and temperature ranges where the primary source of error is the inability to capture diverse liquid configurations. Its effectiveness may be reduced in systems with extreme chemical heterogeneity beyond typical five-component alloys or under conditions where vibrational contributions (at lower temperatures) dominate the free-energy error.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative improvement in phase-space overlap is well motivated, the exact quantitative reduction in integration path mismatch (e.g., the precise percentage improvement) remains uncertain until validated by comparative free-energy calculations.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform parallel thermodynamic integration studies on a representative high-entropy alloy system using (a) the conventional TOR-TILD EAM reference and (b) the newly developed actively learned ML potential. Independently benchmark the free energies using an ab initio method (such as vibrational entropy computed from displacement covariance analysis).
measurements: Free energy differences in the solid and liquid phases
Statistical error (integration path mismatch) quantified for both EAM and ML potential based integrations
Comparison of phase-space overlap metrics (e.g., distribution of atomic configurations) between reference and ab initio ensembles
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ML potential does not yield a statistically significant reduction (for example, less than a 10% improvement) in integration path mismatch relative to the EAM approach, or if the computed free energies do not converge closer to the ab initio benchmark (within experimental error), then the hypothesis is falsified.

Ab initio framework for deciphering trade-off relationships in multi-component alloys

Abstract: While first-principles methods have been successfully applied to characterize individual properties of multi-principal element alloys (MPEA), their use in searching for optimal trade-offs between competing properties is hampered by high computational demands. In this work, we present a framework to explore Pareto-optimal compositions by integrating advanced ab initio-based techniques into a Bayesian multi-objective optimization workflow, complemented by a simple analytical model providing straightforward analysis of trends. Melting simulations of high-entropy carbonitrides by deep learning potentials

Abstract: The melting temperature is a crucial property of materials that determines their potential applications in different industrial fields. In this study, we used a deep neural network potential to describe the structure of high-entropy (TiZrTaHfNb)CxN1−x carbonitrides (HECN) in both solid and liquid states. This approach allows us to predict heating and cooling temperatures depending on the nitrogen content to determine the melting temperature and analyze structure changes from atomistic point of view. A steady increase in nitrogen content leads to increasing melting temperature, with a maximum approaching for 25% of nitrogen in the HECN. A careful analysis of pair correlations, together with calculations of entropy in the considered liquid phases of HECNs allows us to explain the origin of the nonlinear enhancement of the melting temperature with increasing nitrogen content. The maximum melting temperature of 3580 ± 30 K belongs to (TiZrTaHfNb)C0.75N0.25 composition.
